common_name: Silex Heuffelii Hens and Chicks (Clumping Hardy Succulent)

planting.note: Lift and split established clumps in spring or fall and press divisions onto lean, gritty, sharp-draining soil; heuffelii types build new heads by splitting the mother rosette rather than throwing stolon-borne offsets.

directions: Grow in lean, mineral, sharply drained soil in full sun, keeping the crown dry in winter. Silex is a registered Jovibarba heuffelii selection, part of the non-stoloniferous clumping group of hardy hens and chicks that increases by the mother rosette splitting into new crowns rather than sending out runners. Established clumps can be lifted and divided every few seasons to make new plantings or fill gaps in a trough or rock garden. It shares the group's reliable cold hardiness and shares its aversion to standing winter moisture, which is a greater threat than cold itself.

common_name: Pink Star Heuffelii Hens and Chicks (Clumping Hardy Succulent)

planting.note: Divide established clumps in spring or fall and set the separated crowns onto lean, fast-draining gritty soil; this heuffelii selection clumps tightly rather than spreading on stolons.

directions: Plant in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun and avoid soggy winter conditions. Pink Star is a registered Jovibarba heuffelii cultivar, also listed in trade under the older synonym Sempervivum heuffelii; like other heuffelii-type hens and chicks it forms a dense clump that expands by the mother rosette dividing into fresh crowns rather than by producing offsets on runners. This clumping habit makes it a good candidate for crevice plantings and troughs where sprawling sempervivum would quickly outgrow their neighbors. Lift and separate crowns every few years to keep the planting vigorous.

common_name: Try Me Heuffelii Hens and Chicks (Clumping Hardy Succulent)

planting.note: Separate mature clumps into individual crowns in spring or fall and press them onto lean, sharply drained gritty soil rather than sowing seed.

directions: Site in lean, gritty, well-drained soil in full sun with dry winter footing. Try Me is a registered Jovibarba heuffelii cultivar that follows the growth pattern typical of the group: a slowly thickening clump built from the mother rosette splitting into new heads rather than by stoloniferous offsets. Because the clump increases this way, propagation is by division of established crowns rather than by detaching runner-borne plantlets. It carries the same extreme cold hardiness and drought tolerance common to heuffelii-type hens and chicks, needing only sharp drainage to perform well in a rock garden or trough.

common_name: Charell Heuffelii Hens and Chicks (Clumping Hardy Succulent)

planting.note: Divide established clumps in spring or fall and set separated crowns onto lean, gritty, sharply drained soil.

directions: Grow in sharply drained, mineral-lean soil in full sun, keeping plants dry underfoot through winter. Charell is a registered Jovibarba heuffelii selection and shares the group's defining clumping habit, in which the original rosette divides from within to form new crowns instead of spreading by stolon-borne offsets as true Sempervivum do. This makes mature clumps a source of divisions for propagating new plants rather than a source of detachable chicks. It is reliably cold hardy and far more sensitive to wet, poorly drained soil than to winter temperatures.

common_name: Angel Wings Heuffelii Hens and Chicks (Purple-Red Edged-Green Clumping Succulent)

planting.note: Divide established clumps in spring or fall and set separated crowns into lean, gritty, well-drained soil; takes two to five seasons to build a full-sized clump.

directions: Plant in loam or sandy, lean, well-drained soil in full sun and shield the crowns from excess winter wet. Angel Wings is a registered Jovibarba heuffelii cultivar with broad, sharply pointed leaves that are purple-red through the center and rimmed in green, giving each rosette a two-toned, feathered look that inspired the cultivar name. Short spikes of pale yellow bell-shaped flowers can appear above the foliage in summer. Like other heuffelii types it clumps by the mother rosette dividing into new crowns, so propagate by splitting established clumps rather than detaching stolon-borne offsets.

common_name: Summer King Heuffelii Hens and Chicks (Clumping Hardy Succulent)

planting.note: Divide established clumps in spring or fall and press separated crowns onto lean, sharply drained gritty soil.

directions: Site in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun with a dry winter position. Summer King is a registered Jovibarba heuffelii selection that follows the group's characteristic growth pattern, where the original rosette gradually splits into multiple crowns rather than producing stolon-borne chicks. Mature clumps can be lifted and divided to propagate new plants or to refresh a crowded planting. As with other heuffelii cultivars, it tolerates hard winter cold readily but suffers if left standing in wet soil.

common_name: Dunbar Red Heuffelii Hens and Chicks (Clumping Hardy Succulent)

planting.note: Divide established clumps in spring or fall and press separated crowns onto lean, gritty, well-drained soil; also listed in trade as Jovibarba hirta 'Dunbar Red'.

directions: Grow in lean, mineral, sharply drained soil in full sun, keeping the crown on the dry side over winter. Dunbar Red is a registered Jovibarba heuffelii cultivar also catalogued under the closely related name Jovibarba hirta 'Dunbar Red', reflecting some ongoing disagreement in the trade over which heuffelii-group species certain selections belong to. Regardless of the exact species label, it grows and clumps the same way as other hardy heuffelii-type hens and chicks, with the mother rosette dividing into new crowns rather than spreading on runners. Divide established clumps every few years to propagate or to keep the planting vigorous.

common_name: Nobel Heuffelii Hens and Chicks (Clumping Hardy Succulent)

planting.note: Divide established clumps in spring or fall and set separated crowns onto lean, gritty, sharply drained soil.

directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained gritty soil in full sun and avoid letting the crown sit wet over winter. Nobel is a registered Jovibarba heuffelii cultivar with jade-green, fringe-edged rosettes that grows true to the group's clumping habit, increasing as the mother rosette divides into fresh crowns rather than by sending out stolon-borne chicks the way true Sempervivum do. This makes established clumps a ready source of divisions for starting new plantings. It shares the heuffelii group's reliable winter hardiness and low tolerance for soggy soil.

planting.note: Set offset rosettes into lean, well-drained soil in spring or fall; forms a tight evergreen mat over two to five seasons.

directions: Plant in lean, well-drained soil of almost any composition in full sun or light partial shade. Rosularia muratdaghensis, native to Turkey's Murat Dağı mountains and named for botanist Peter Davis's 1962 collection there, forms small, slightly fuzzy rosettes of fleshy green leaves tipped in red that tighten into a dense evergreen mat over a few seasons. In summer, short stems rise above the foliage carrying clusters of small tubular flowers in creamy white to soft yellow. It is a tough rock-garden and trough succulent that tolerates both acid and alkaline soils as long as drainage is sharp, and it is hardy through severe winters where the planting stays dry.

planting.note: Set offset rosettes into lean, sharply drained soil in spring or fall; also sold under the current accepted name Prometheum serpentinicum.

directions: Grow in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun to bright partial shade. Native to Turkey, Rosularia serpentinica forms small, tight rosettes resembling a miniature hen-and-chicks, with dark green leaves that take on a bronze-red cast in cool weather and deepen to dull red through summer heat. It stays compact, making it a good choice for trough gardens, tufa, and crevice plantings where larger succulents would crowd out neighboring alpines. Keep it dry through winter, since the main risk to this species in cold climates is prolonged soil moisture rather than low temperatures.
